strings: Agamaggan the Great Boar was one of the colossal Ancient Guardians who walked Azeroth in its earliest days. He fell ten thousand years ago fighting the Burning Legion in the War of the Ancients, sacrificing his life so mortals could reach the Well of Eternity. Where his blood and body crashed into the earth, vast networks of thorny vines arose, creating the Razorfen and granting life and purpose to his descendants, the quilboar.

Ten thousand years ago, during the first invasion of the Burning Legion, the demigod Cenarius rallied the Ancient Guardians to aid the night elves in defending Azeroth. Agamaggan answered the call with terrifying ferocity. Towering over the battlefield, the Great Boar trampled legions of doomguards under his massive hooves, exhaled streams of caustic breath, and launched salvos of razor-sharp thorns from his bristling back. His warpath carried him across the continent, where he clashed directly against demonic generals such as Mannoroth. Ultimately overwhelmed by sheer numbers, Agamaggan fought to his dying breath, buying Malfurion Stormrage and the kaldorei resistance precious time to reach the Well of Eternity.

Where Agamaggan collapsed in the southern Barrens, his colossal corpse reshaped the land. His spilled blood soaked into the soil, causing enormous, impenetrable brambles and thorny vines to burst upward from the dry earth. These tangled thickets became known as the Razorfen. The quilboar revere the site as their holiest ground, viewing the labyrinth of Razorfen Kraul as his resting body and Razorfen Downs as his gaping skull. Scattered throughout the Barrens are crystallized Blood Shards, believed to be the physical remnants of the demigod's spilled blood, pulsing with lingering primal energy that quilboar geomancers and shamans harness for power.

Agamaggan is revered as the divine progenitor of all quilboar. They view the surrounding brambles not merely as homes, but as the living armor left behind by their creator to shelter them from hostile neighbors. Quilboar tribes believe their god's spirit watches over them, granting martial vigor to their warriors and earth magic to their geomancers. In turn, they aggressively defend the thorns against encroaching tauren, orcs, and centaur, convinced that their sacred duty is to guard the fallen body of the boar god who birthed them.

The Alliance is a grand coalition of mortal races bound by shared ideals of honor, duty, and the defense of order across Azeroth. Born out of the ashes of the northern kingdom of Lordaeron, its current heart beats in Stormwind City, united alongside the dwarves of Ironforge, the exiled gnomes, and the night elves of Kalimdor.

The modern Alliance descends from the original Alliance of Lordaeron, founded when Sir Anduin Lothar led Stormwind refugees north during the Second War to unite the Seven Kingdoms, dwarves, and high elves against the Old Horde. While the Scourge and the Third War decimated the north—leaving Lordaeron in ruins and driving the survivors into scattered resistance—the restored Kingdom of Stormwind rose to fill the void. Today, Stormwind stands as the preeminent seat of human leadership, carrying the banners of honor and faith into a fractured world.
A Coalition of Necessity and Kinship

The faction's backbone in the Eastern Kingdoms relies on the steadfast bond between humans and the dwarves of Ironforge under King Magni Bronzebeard. Alongside the dwarves reside the gnomes, driven from Gnomeregan by a devastating trogg uprising. Guided by High Tinker Gelbin Mekkatorque, the exiled gnomes lend their brilliant engineering to the Alliance war effort, believing the coalition's survival is paramount to ever reclaiming their irradiated home.

Across the Great Sea, the reclusive night elves abandoned millennia of isolation after the Battle of Mount Hyjal. Reeling from the loss of their immortality and engaged in bitter territorial clashes against the Horde over logging in Ashenvale, the kaldorei allied with their newfound mortal companions. Though cultural friction remains—and some traditionalists decry the presence of humans and dwarves in ancient forests—the Alliance provides vital military and diplomatic cooperation to safeguard Kalimdor against demonic remnants and Horde expansion.

Despite its outward strength, the Alliance is beset by internal strain. King Varian Wrynn vanished under mysterious circumstances en route to a diplomatic summit, leaving his young son Anduin on the throne under Highlord Bolvar Fordragon's regency. Relations with former human allies are fractured: the maritime kingdom of Kul Tiras keeps its distance, while Sylvanas Windrunner's undead Forsaken now hold the ruins of Lordaeron.

The Alliance of Lordaeron was the historic grand coalition of the seven human kingdoms, Khaz Modan dwarves, Wildhammer gryphon riders, gnomes, and high elves formed to resist the Old Horde in the Second War. Led militarily by Supreme Commander Anduin Lothar and diplomatically by King Terenas Menethil II, it shattered the invading orcish forces and secured the Eastern Kingdoms. Though political fractures and the devastation of the Scourge tore it apart during the Third War, its legacy laid the foundation for the current Alliance.

Following the horrific sack of Stormwind in the First War, Regent Lord Anduin Lothar brought the battered southern refugees across the Great Sea to Capital City. Pleading their cause before King Terenas Menethil II, the leaders of the north assembled as the Council of Seven Nations. Old rivalries, border tensions, and isolationism—especially from Gilneas and Alterac—threatened to doom the summit before it began. It took urgent word of the Horde conquering Khaz Modan and an impassioned plea from the priest Turalyon to shake the rulers from their complacency. Choosing Lothar as their neutral Supreme Commander, the seven human nations bound themselves together in a desperate pact.
The Second War and the New Vanguard

Facing brutal orcish warriors, dark warlocks, and monstrous red dragons, the Alliance forged entirely new doctrines of war. Archbishop Alonsus Faol and Lothar established the Knights of the Silver Hand, elevating holy paladins like Uther the Lightbringer and Tirion Fordring to counter the Horde's dark magic. When the war raged across the Hinterlands and quelled the siege of Aerie Peak, Kurdran Wildhammer pledged his fierce gryphon riders to rule the skies. Shortly thereafter, the Bronzebeard dwarves and Gnomeregan gnomes were liberated, joining high elven rangers under Alleria Windrunner. Despite the treacherous betrayal of King Perenolde of Alterac, the grand coalition drove the Horde back to Blackrock Spire and crushed their dominion.

Victory brought bitterness rather than enduring peace. Bitter disputes erupted over the high taxes required to maintain the orc internment camps and rebuild the blasted kingdom of Stormwind. Seeing little personal gain, Gilneas built the Greymane Wall and severed ties, Stromgarde departed over territorial and prisoner quarrels, and Quel'Thalas pulled back behind its enchanted runestones. The coalition that remained under King Terenas attempted to weather the political storm, only to be utterly dismantled during the Third War when the Cult of the Damned and the Plague of Undeath swept across Lordaeron. Arthas Menethil's betrayal tore the heart out of the kingdom, ending the golden age of the northern realm.

Alterac was one of the seven historic human kingdoms, nestled high in the rugged Alterac Mountains. During the Second War, its ruler, King Aiden Perenolde, made a treacherous pact with the Old Horde to spare his realm, leading to the kingdom's military downfall and total collapse. Today, its ruined capital lies abandoned in the snow, while dispossessed nobles and outlaws wage a guerrilla war under the banner of the Syndicate.

Alterac arose thousands of years ago as an Arathorian city-state following the Troll Wars. Settlers capitalized on strategic mountain passes and trading outposts, eventually establishing an independent realm when the empire fractured. Though rugged and mountainous, Alterac bordered the prosperous lands of Lordaeron and Stromgarde, extending as far as the shores of Darrowmere Lake. Historically, it fielded tough mountain fighters, but enduring border friction with Thoras Trollbane's Stromgarde left the kingdom politically isolated from its neighbors long before the Dark Portal ever opened.

When Sir Anduin Lothar forged the Alliance of Lordaeron, King Aiden Perenolde joined only with deep reluctance. As Orgrim Doomhammer's Horde swept north, Perenolde concluded humanity was doomed and secretly struck a deal with the Warchief. In exchange for the safety of Alterac, Perenolde opened fortified mountain passes, conspired against Alliance forces, and even dispatched soldiers and sailors to assist the Horde's siege of Lordaeron. The treachery allowed the orcs to reach Capital City far ahead of schedule, shaking the Alliance to its core when the truth was laid bare.

Retribution was swift. Stromgarde's forces marched into the mountains, exposing Perenolde's treason and breaking Alterac's military. King Terenas Menethil II placed the fallen nation under martial law, while arguments over who should inherit the throne paralyzed Alliance diplomats for years. Following the kingdom's collapse, King Perenolde died in disgrace. His son, Lord Aliden Perenolde, rallied the bitter, displaced nobility to form the Syndicate. Wearing the orange cloth of their fallen homeland, these bandits and mercenaries now fight ruthlessly to reclaim their ancestral holdings across Hillsbrad and Alterac.

Sir Anduin Lothar, known as the Lion of Stormwind, was the last descendant of the ancient Arathi bloodline and the Supreme Commander of the Alliance of Lordaeron. A childhood companion of King Llane Wrynn and the Guardian Medivh, Lothar led humanity through the horrors of the First War and rallied the northern nations during the Second War before falling at Blackrock Mountain.

Carrying the ancient bloodline of the Arathi kings, Lothar grew up within Stormwind's royal court alongside Prince Llane Wrynn and Medivh. The trio embarked on reckless excursions into the wilderness, skirmishing with Gurubashi trolls in Stranglethorn Vale. Lothar rose rapidly through Stormwind's martial ranks, joining the King's Honor Guard and earning renown as an Armsman of the Brotherhood of the Horse.

When mysterious green-skinned invaders poured from the Black Morass, King Llane named Lothar the King's Champion to mount the kingdom's defense. Lothar pioneered devastating ambushes against orcish raiding parties across Westfall, the Redridge Mountains, and Elwynn Forest, outmaneuvering Warchief Blackhand and breaking the first siege of Stormwind City. Yet betrayal doomed the kingdom from within: Medivh was revealed as the architect who opened the Dark Portal, compelling Lothar and the apprentice Khadgar to storm Karazhan and execute the corrupted Guardian. Returning to find King Llane assassinated and Stormwind burning, Lothar gathered the survivors—including young Prince Varian—and evacuated them north across the Great Sea.

Arriving on the shores of Lordaeron, Lothar presented the grim reality of the Horde to King Terenas Menethil II. Invoking his ancestral Arathi lineage and diplomatic gravitas, he unified the human realms, Ironforge dwarves, and high elves into the Grand Alliance of Lordaeron. Named Supreme Commander of the united forces, Lothar spearheaded the campaign that pushed the Horde back south to the foot of Blackrock Mountain. There, in a fateful clash near the end of the Second War, Lothar was slain by Warchief Orgrim Doomhammer. His death did not shatter the Alliance; instead, it galvanized his lieutenant, Turalyon, to lead the charge that broke the Horde forever.

The Argent Dawn is a neutral, knightly order dedicated to stamping out malevolent threats across Azeroth, most notably the Scourge and the Burning Legion. Formed by survivors of the Knights of the Silver Hand who rejected the fanatical zealotry of the Scarlet Crusade, they welcome champions of any race or faction who honor the cause of the Light. From their fortified sanctuary at Light's Hope Chapel to far-flung outposts across Kalimdor, they stand on the front lines against darkness.

When Highlord Alexandros Mograine fell and Lordaeron collapsed into ruin, the shattered remnants of the Knights of the Silver Hand broke into bitter disagreement. Many survivors surrendered to grief and paranoia, morphing into the xenophobic Scarlet Crusade. Yet veterans like Lord Maxwell Tyrosus and Pureheart recognized that their former comrades had abandoned the true tenets of the Holy Light. Refusing to succumb to madness or abandon the dead kingdom, they split away to form the Argent Dawn—an order committed to defending Azeroth alongside anyone willing to fight, whether Alliance or Horde.

The Dawn's primary stronghold is Light's Hope Chapel, situated in the blighted expanse of the Eastern Plaguelands. From this consecrated bastion, the order coordinates an unending war against Kel'Thuzad's necromancers and skeletal legions. Operating forward camps at Chillwind Camp and outside the Bulwark in Tirisfal Glades, Argent officers issue enchanted commissions to adventurers, paying bounties in exchange for Scourgestones wrested from fallen undead. Despite lacking the raw manpower of the Scarlet Crusade, the Dawn holds the line through perseverance, unity, and unshakable discipline.

While Lordaeron remains their principal battleground, the Argent Dawn maintains an active watch across Kalimdor and the capitals of the world. They keep diplomatic presences in Stormwind City, Darnassus, and the goblin trade town of Everlook. Farther afield, operatives like Delgren the Purifier contest demonic cults in Darkshore and Ashenvale, while scouts in Desolace and the flooded ruins of Blackfathom Deeps investigate sinister threats involving the Shadow Council and the Twilight's Hammer cult.

Facing annihilation by the Scourge, a pragmatic sect within the order known as the Brotherhood of the Light strives to maintain a cold truce with the Scarlet Crusade. Yet relations remain deeply strained. High-ranking officers like Duke Nicholas Zverenhoff actively sanction covert strikes against Scarlet leadership in Stratholme to purge what they view as heretical madness. Compounding their perils, dark forces relentlessly seek to infiltrate the Dawn's ranks—including secret agents who siphon necromantic secrets from the front lines for treacherous masters elsewhere.

The Clerics of the First War

Centuries ago, pious missionaries traveled south from Lordaeron into the kingdom of Stormwind, establishing Northshire Abbey to minister to the people and soothe the realm through the Holy Light. Originally known as the Holy Order of Northshire Clerics, their compassion was legendary—they even tended to injured gnolls and jungle trolls during past border wars. When the Orcish Horde crossed through the Dark Portal, the clerics marched bravely to the front lines without armor or weapons to heal fallen soldiers. Because their healing sustained the Stormwind Army, the orcs ruthlessly targeted them. The order was decimated, the abbey was ransacked and burned, and the surviving clerics were forced to flee north across the sea to Southshore with Sir Anduin Lothar.

The slaughter of the Northshire clerics sent shockwaves through the human kingdoms. Realizing that faith alone could not withstand an axe without armor and martial discipline, Archbishop Alonsus Faol resolved to create warriors who possessed both the sacred powers of the Light and the martial mastery of a knight. Drawing upon the surviving clerics and devout knights, Faol formed the Knights of the Silver Hand, giving rise to humanity's first paladins. In this way, the sacrifice of Northshire's fallen healers became the very foundation for the holy warriors who broke the Horde in the Second War.

The Burning Legion is an infinite, apocalyptic host of demons led by the fallen titan Sargeras, dedicated to scouring all life from creation. Having already shattered ancient Kalimdor ten thousand years ago, the demons remain Azeroth's most relentless nemesis, orchestrating the corruption of the orcs and the horrors of the Third War.

Long ago, Sargeras stood as the champion of the titans, tasked with hunting down and imprisoning the demons that plagued the cosmos. Over countless ages of battling their evil, he grew disillusioned and concluded that creation itself was fatally flawed and must be unmade in flame. To enact his crusade, he freed the demons he had imprisoned, bending them to his will through fel magic. The catastrophic implosion tore the supercontinent apart in the Great Sundering, casting the ruined lands across vast new seas.

Centaur are a violent, horse-bodied humanoid race whose nomadic clans dominate the arid plains of central Kalimdor. Born from the tragic union between the demigod Zaetar and the earth princess Theradras, they spent centuries driving the tauren toward extinction before the newly arrived orcish Horde intervened.

Centaur originated roughly eleven hundred years ago beneath the wastes of Desolace. When Princess Theradras, daughter of the elemental lord Therazane, awoke and withered the surrounding land, the demigod Zaetar arrived from the Emerald Dream to investigate. The two formed an unnatural union, and their offspring emerged as the first centaur. Horrified by their misshapen, savage nature, Zaetar could not hide his revulsion. Enraged by their father's disgust, the centaur slaughtered him. Though grief-stricken Theradras entombed Zaetar's spirit within her subterranean sanctuary of Maraudon, she shielded and nurtured her vicious children, who swiftly multiplied across Kalimdor.

Following their emergence, the centaur expanded outward from Desolace, waging a brutal war of attrition against Kalimdor's native populations. The nomadic tauren suffered the most: driven from their fertile ancestral homeland of Mulgore, they were chased relentlessly across the Barrens. Centaur warbands treated the tauren as prey, burning settlements and hunting them for sport. By the time of the Third War, centuries of relentless pursuit had brought the tauren to the precipice of extinction, leaving them desperately fleeing endless marauders across the savannah.

Everything shifted when Warchief Thrall and the newly arrived orcish Horde landed upon Kalimdor. Thrall formed a pact with Cairne Bloodhoof, uniting orcish steel with tauren might. Together, they crushed the aggressive Kolkar warbands, broke their grip on the plains, and enabled the tauren to safely establish Thunder Bluff and reclaim Mulgore. This alliance ended the nomadic exile of the tauren and established a debt of blood and honor that permanently bound them into the Horde.

Despite their staggering defeats, centaur remain an active threat across central Kalimdor. Their society is divided into warring clans—primarily the Kolkar, Gelkis, Magram, and Maraudine—each led by a khan and locked in perpetual blood feuds over territory and water. While their internal squabbles keep them from uniting into an unstoppable horde, aggressive raiding parties continue to strike at trade caravans and settlements across Durotar, the Barrens, Thousand Needles, and the borders of Mulgore.

The Cult of the Damned is a secretive cabal of mortal zealots, necromancers, and aristocrats devoted to the Lich King. The Cult of the Damned was forged by the exiled Archmage Kel'Thuzad after he answered the telepathic whispers of the Lich King emanating from the Frozen Throne. Returning to Lordaeron with vast wealth and forbidden dark arts, Kel'Thuzad offered two false gospels: to the desperate, impoverished lower classes, he promised social equality and liberation from misery; to the wealthy landowners, such as the noble House of Barov, he promised eternal life and an unshakeable grip upon their domains. In truth, both the destitute and the affluent were cattle intended for slaughter, bound into a death cult designed to betray their homeland from the inside.

Operating in complete secrecy from the dungeons beneath Caer Darrow, the cultists honed their necrotic craft, built hulking abominations, and perfected the Plague of Undeath brought south from Northrend. They struck at Lordaeron's breadbasket, contaminating the grain stores at Andorhal. As tainted flour traveled through regular merchant routes to hearths across the Eastweald, commoners sickened and died within days, only to rise as shambling thralls under the Lich King's telepathic lash. When Prince Arthas slaughtered Kel'Thuzad in Andorhal, the cultist network was already so deeply rooted that the kingdom's doom was sealed.

Long ago, three dwarven factions lived together in Ironforge under High King Modimus Anvilmar. When the king died, civil war erupted. The Bronzebeards defeated both rival factions, casting out the Wildhammers and Sorcerer-Thane Thaurissan's Dark Irons. His ritual breached the core of the world and freed Ragnaros the Firelord.

The rebirth of Ragnaros violently shattered the surrounding peaks, carving out the blazing caldera of Blackrock Mountain flanked by the Searing Gorge and the Burning Steppes. The sorcerer-thane perished in the cataclysm, and the surviving Dark Irons found themselves bound into perpetual servitude to the Firelord. Over centuries within the lower chambers of the mountain, they constructed the sprawling subterranean capital of Shadowforge City. Their artisans and sorcerers became masters of stone golems, dark sorceries, and steam-driven siege machinery, weaponizing the molten elements around them under the gaze of flamewakers and elemental overlords.

The Defias Brotherhood is a widespread criminal network of bandits, brigands, and assassins waging an underground insurgency against the Kingdom of Stormwind. Originally formed by the artisans of the Stonemasons Guild who were cheated of their pay for rebuilding the capital, they have devolved into violent outlaws terrorizing the southern farmlands. From their hidden redoubt deep beneath Westfall, they aim to overthrow the corrupt House of Nobles and lay waste to the kingdom.

Following the Second War, the Stonemasons Guild was hired to rebuild Stormwind from smoldering ruins into a grand stone capital. When their masterwork was finished, the House of Nobles refused to deliver the promised payment, citing crushing wartime debt. Guildmaster Edwin VanCleef spoke out on behalf of his workers, demanding fair restitution, but the nobles responded by ordering the Stonemasons Guild disbanded. The ensuing riots in the city streets turned tragic when a stray rock struck and killed Queen Tiffin Wrynn. Overcome with grief and rage, King Varian Wrynn drove the laborers out of Stormwind into exile. Stripped of their livelihood and outlawed, VanCleef and the desperate workers banded together, binding their faces in red silk to represent the blood of the wronged, and turned to highway robbery to claim what they believed they were owed.

With the royal army overextended, VanCleef turned the neglected farmlands of Westfall into the Brotherhood's base of operations. The bandits overran the hamlet of Moonbrook and commandeered the abandoned subterranean tunnels of the Deadmines. Defias agents seized local mines, driven farmers from their homesteads with reprogrammed harvest golems, and salted the earth to starve the region. With the Crown unable or unwilling to send soldiers to protect rural citizens, local farmers formed The People's Militia out of Sentinel Hill to fight a desperate war of attrition against an enemy that now outmans and outguns them.

The Brotherhood has long outgrown a simple band of displaced laborers. VanCleef recruited mercenary goblins to oversee armaments, struck alliances with Riverpaw gnolls and Elwynn kobolds, and traded with cutthroat pirates like the Bloodsail Buccaneers. Defias highwaymen raid gold shipments across Elwynn Forest, and their agents even established a foothold in Duskwood before unearthing a cursed artifact in Roland's Doom. Far worse, the Brotherhood's influence reaches into the very heart of the capital, enjoying covert support from treacherous aristocrats within the House of Nobles while orchestrating kidnappings that strike at the highest offices of the Alliance.

Beneath Moonbrook lies the Ironclad Cove, where VanCleef's goblin engineers are secretly assembling an enormous iron-plated warship known as the Defias Juggernaught. The guildmaster intends to sail this floating fortress out through the subterranean coastal waterways and bombard Stormwind City from the sea, reducing his own grand architecture to rubble. The conspiracy extends into the royal court itself: corrupt nobles like Lord Gregor Lescovar serve as eyes and ears for the uprising, while the court machinations of Lady Katrana Prestor deliberately keep the kingdom fractured and blind to the rising fleet beneath Westfall.

Guided by whispers from the black dragon Deathwing, the clan's chieftain, Zuluhed the Whacked, recovered an ancient golden disk from the Redridge Mountains: the Dragon Soul. Using the artifact's agonizing power, Nekros ensnared Alexstrasza the Life-Binder herself. The Dragonmaw fortified the abandoned dwarven bastion of Grim Batol, keeping the Dragonqueen chained in darkness and forcing her red dragon brood to serve the Old Horde as aerial dreadnoughts during the Second War.

Routed and terrified, the surviving Dragonmaw scattered into the marshy bogs of the Wetlands and the jagged peaks around Grim Batol. The remnants on Azeroth live as desperate, feral renegades, fiercely guarding their dwindling encampments against dwarven patrols and vengeful dragons alike.

Druids are guardians of the natural world who draw power directly from the wild spirits, the celestial bodies, and the Emerald Dream. Master shapeshifters, they adopt the forms of primal beasts to protect the land or mend grievous wounds. Practiced primarily by the night elves and newly revived among the tauren, druids place the preservation of nature above all mortal allegiance.

Druidism is far more than a martial art; it is an ancient way of life rooted in deep communion with nature and the demigod Cenarius. Druids wield raw natural energies, commanding roots to entangle their foes, directing the celestial brilliance of the moon and stars, and invoking restorative flora to knit bone and flesh. Their duty is to preserve the cosmic balance and protect the unfettered wild from exploitation and corruption.

The defining hallmark of the druid is the supernatural art of shapeshifting. Through spiritual devotion, practitioners channel the primal aspects of Azeroth's beasts. They take on the thick hide of the bear to withstand crushing assaults, slip into the lithe form of the feline predator to strike from the shadows, or adopt aquatic and avian shapes to traverse sea and sky. While transformed, their animal mouths can rarely form mortal words, yet their physical prowess rivals the apex predators of the wild.

First taught to Malfurion Stormrage by Cenarius ten thousand years ago, mortal druidism was later formalized under the Cenarion Circle. Headquartered in sacred Moonglade, the Circle watches over druidic practices across Kalimdor, standing independent of mortal factions and political squabbles. While long dominated solely by night elf men who spent centuries slumbering in the Emerald Dream, the aftermath of the Third War saw both night elf women and the tauren welcomed into its fold.

Something went horribly awry inside Naralex's trance. Instead of channeling the pristine serenity of the Emerald Dream, Naralex’s slumber was infiltrated by a malevolent, twisting nightmare. Dwarves are a stout, resilient race carved from the living stone of ancient titan-forged earthen, now inhabiting the snow-capped mountain kingdoms of Khaz Modan and beyond. Known for their mastery of stonework, metallurgy, and devastating frontline combat, they stand as one of the Alliance's fiercest and most dependable pillars. Under the reign of King Magni Bronzebeard, their sprawling subterranean capital of Ironforge serves as the beating heart of dwarven society.

Long ago, the subterranean titan-forged known as earthen awoke from an eons-long slumber within the vaults of Uldaman, transformed by the Curse of Flesh into beings of blood and bone. Taking the name dwarves, they reclaimed the high crags of Khaz Modan—named in honor of the titan Khaz'goroth—and carved the majestic subterranean stronghold of Ironforge beneath the peaks of Dun Morogh. Endowed with incredible natural fortitude, a sharp eye for stone and ore, and a penchant for roaring hearths and heady ale, dwarves approach craftsmanship and warfare with identical tenacity.
The War of the Three Hammers

Dwarven unity shattered centuries ago following the death of High King Modimus Anvilmar. Civil war erupted across Ironforge among three rival factions: the Bronzebeard clan, the Wildhammer clan, and the Dark Iron clan. After the Bronzebeards secured the mountain and drove out their kin, Sorcerer-Thane Thaurissan of the Dark Irons launched a disastrous war of vengeance against both rivals. Driven to desperation beneath the Redridge Mountains, Thaurissan accidentally summoned Ragnaros the Firelord, immolating his own realm into the volcanic wastes of Searing Gorge and the Burning Steppes. The surviving Dark Irons were enslaved beneath Blackrock Mountain, while the devastated Wildhammers migrated north to Aerie Peak in the Hinterlands.

When the orcish Horde surged across the continent during the Second War, King Magni Bronzebeard sealed Ironforge's gates against brutal sieges while dwarven forces took up arms alongside the Alliance of Lordaeron. Renowned for heavy plate armor, deadly muskets, and fearless gryphon riders, dwarven warriors played a vital role in shattering the Horde. Today, the Kingdom of Ironforge remains one of the Alliance's most stalwart defenders, welcoming their displaced gnome cousins into their halls while actively unearthing the titan ruins of Khaz Modan to unravel the mysteries of their ancient origins.

The Earth Mother is the supreme, benevolent creator deity worshipped by the tauren, revered as the living embodiment and architect of Azeroth's land and elements. In tauren myth, she shaped the mountains, plains, and seasons and set the sun and moon in the sky as her watchful eyes. Her presence permeates everyday tauren culture, guiding their reverence for nature, duty to the elements, and hopes for the afterlife.

Tauren creation myths tell that before day and night existed, the Earth Mother set about shaping Azeroth as a haven for her coming children. Scraping her nails across newly raised mountains sparked the world's first fires, while her hands carved rivers and ocean beds. Her laughter gave breath to the wind, and by lifting the primordial fogs into the sky, she brought the first rains, which coaxed grass, forests, and grain from the soil.

Aided by the friendly elements, the Earth Mother brought forth twins: An'she, the sun, and Mu'sha, the moon. To rest while keeping them safe, she placed the radiant twins into her eyes, creating day, night, and the cycle of the seasons as she opened and closed each lid. Later, she pressed her heart against the fertile earth, breathing the song of life into the land to create the shu'halo, the first tauren. She charged the twins and the elements with teaching the young mortals how to hunt, build, dance, and live in harmony with the wilds.

In time, the Earth Mother set An'she and Mu'sha in the sky, where the sun and moon keep watch over the land by day and by night. Tauren say that her spirit now dwells in the rivers, trees, plains, and mountains of the world, and that every lesser nature spirit springs from her and returns to her in the end.

Tauren believe her spirit cradles Azeroth still. Her ear is attuned to the winds, hearing the prayers of her children, and her heart beats within the deep stone. Tauren hunters, shamans, and druids direct their thanks to her for every kill and harvest, believing that all life originates from her embrace and that every tauren's spirit returns to her soil upon death.

The Elemental Plane is an interconnected pocket dimension forged by the titan-forged Keepers to imprison Azeroth's chaotic elementals. Divided into four distinct realms—Skywall, Deepholm, the Abyssal Maw, and the Firelands—it confines the primordial spirits away from the mortal world. Though sealed long ago, cracks in its barriers allow violent elemental incursions and catastrophic summonings into Azeroth.

In the ancient days following the fall of the Old Gods, the titan-forged Keepers faced a dilemma: Azeroth's chaotic elementals could not truly be destroyed, as their essences were fundamentally tied to the world. The Keepers devised an enduring solution by weaving an isolated pocket dimension known as the Elemental Plane. Within it, they crafted four interlinked domains tailored to each primal force: Skywall for air, Deepholm for earth, the Abyssal Maw for water, and the Firelands for fire. The elemental lords and their myriad servants were banished into this realm, and powerful wards were set to sever the prison from the material world, allowing Azeroth's surface to finally know peace.

Banishment did not temper the fury of the elementals. Confined within their pocket dimensions, the primordial powers waged endless wars against one another. The most terrible conflict, the Elemental Sundering, pitted the domains of fire and air against each other in a war that raged for millennia across the core of their prison. Meanwhile, a handful of elementals left behind on Azeroth gradually lost their fiery tempestuousness over ages, their forms softening into creatures of flesh and blood.

The barriers separating Azeroth from the Elemental Plane are formidable, but not unbreakable. Two centuries ago, during the desperate climax of the War of the Three Hammers, Sorcerer-Thane Thaurissan pierced the veil to summon Ragnaros the Firelord from the Firelands, an apocalyptic event that ruptured the Redridge Mountains and forged Blackrock Mountain. In recent days, volatile cracks have opened across Kalimdor. Dimensional rifts repeatedly manifest in Silithus, Un'Goro Crater, Azshara, and Winterspring, disgorging waves of hostile elementals eager to test the defenses of the mortal world.

Originally roosting among the crags of the Stonetalon Mountains, they have aggressively migrated across Kalimdor, terrorizing the arid canyons of Durotar, the sacred boughs of Teldrassil, and the heights of Mulgore. The House of Nobles is the hereditary aristocratic council that helps administer the kingdom of Stormwind from Stormwind Keep. Holding immense leverage over regional land, taxation, and trade, their refusal to pay the rebuilt city's laborers ignited the bloody riots that gave birth to the Defias Brotherhood.

Composed of Stormwind's most powerful patrician bloodlines, the House of Nobles serves as the primary advisory body to the Crown. Because the aristocracy owns the majority of the arable land throughout Elwynn, Westfall, and Duskwood, they wield outsized authority over commerce, regional magistrates, and royal decrees. While the boy-king Anduin Wrynn and Highlord Bolvar Fordragon officially rule the kingdom, the council routinely ties the throne's hands in red tape, asserting the power to stall trials, block executions, and meddle in provincial administration.

Following the Second War, the House of Nobles contracted Guildmaster Edwin VanCleef and the Stonemasons Guild to rebuild Stormwind City from its ashes. However, the nobility simultaneously incurred staggering debts while expanding the kingdom's military frontier south into Stranglethorn. When the gleaming capital was finished, the nobles balked at the invoice and refused to pay the workers their full wages. Enraged by the betrayal, the masons rioted in the streets. A stone thrown during the chaos struck and killed Queen Tiffin Wrynn, prompting the nobility to banish the guild, driving the ruined workers into Westfall to form the Defias Brotherhood.

With King Varian missing, the nobles have largely abandoned the kingdom's outlying territories to fend for themselves while exploiting royal authority for petty squabbles. Humans are an adaptable and resilient mortal race who have shaped much of the Eastern Kingdoms' history. Once unified under the ancient Empire of Arathor, their civilization fractured into the Seven Kingdoms, with Stormwind now standing as humanity's primary surviving bastion within the Alliance.

Millennia ago, early humans lived as scattered, nomadic tribes constantly threatened by the Amani forest trolls. Recognizing that disunity would mean extinction, Warlord Thoradin of the Arathi tribe united the disparate clans through diplomacy and conquest, establishing the Empire of Arathor with its fortress capital at Strom. During the Troll Wars, the beleaguered high elves of Quel'Thalas allied with Arathor, teaching one hundred humans the arts of arcane magic. Together, they broke the troll armies, securing humanity's dominion over the central continents and laying the foundation for future mortal alliances.

As Arathor grew secure and prosperous, its outlying settlements became powerful, self-sufficient city-states. Over time, the centralized empire splintered into seven distinct realms: Gilneas, Alterac, Dalaran, Lordaeron, Kul Tiras, Stormwind, and Stromgarde (the original home of Strom). While these nations traded vigorously with dwarves, gnomes, and elves, peace was fragile. Territorial disputes, border skirmishes—such as the perennial mountain feuds between Alterac and Stromgarde—and courtly intrigue consumed the kingdoms, creating deep rivalries that persisted until external catastrophes forced their hand.

The arrival of the orcish Horde through the Dark Portal shattered humanity's internal squabbles. Stormwind was razed during the First War, its refugees fleeing north to warn the other realms. In response, King Terenas Menethil II helped forge the Alliance of Lordaeron, combining the strength of mankind, dwarves, gnomes, and high elves to defeat the Horde in the Second War. Though Stormwind was painstakingly rebuilt, tragedy struck again when the Scourge plague ravaged Lordaeron and Dalaran fell during the Third War, leaving the northern human realms in smoking ruin.

Today, Stormwind stands as the strongest remaining human kingdom and the linchpin of the grand Alliance. However, peace remains elusive. King Varian Wrynn has mysteriously vanished while en route to a diplomatic summit, leaving his ten-year-old son, Anduin Wrynn, crowned king while Highlord Bolvar Fordragon serves as regent. To the north, the survivors of Lordaeron are scattered or dead, while Gilneas hides behind its colossal Greymane Wall, leaving Stormwind to bear the weight of mankind's defense.

Masters of wilderness survival and deadly marksmanship, hunters roam the untamed reaches of Azeroth alongside fierce beast companions. Armed with bows, rifles, or crossbows, they excel at harassing enemies from a distance while relying on clever traps and primal aspects to control the flow of battle. Whether tracking elusive quarry across snowcapped peaks or stalking prey through dense forests, they live by their wits and connection to nature.

At the heart of every hunter lies an instinctual empathy for the primal world. Unlike those who exploit nature or isolate themselves within stone bastions, hunters immerse themselves entirely in untamed lands. They study the habits, movements, and strengths of predatory beasts, earning their respect rather than breaking their spirits. Through patient bonding, a hunter tames dangerous creatures—such as fierce prowling cats, stubborn mountain bears, and sharp-eyed raptors—turning wild animals into steadfast allies that defend them to the death.

On the battlefield, hunters dictate the terms of engagement from a safe distance. Armed with bows, heavy crossbows, or calibrated rifles, they unleash deadly volleys that pierce through heavy armor before an attacker can even draw near. Their finely honed senses make them peerless trackers, capable of tracing the faintest footsteps, scents, and disturbances left by quarry. When foes attempt to close the distance, hunters deploy frost and flame traps, disorienting ambushes, or agile evasive maneuvers to keep enemies right where they want them.

The path of the hunter manifests differently among the various cultures of Azeroth. Night elf Sentinels embody ancient marksmanship and stealth beneath the canopy of Ashenvale, utilizing bows and shadowcraft in quiet harmony with the wilderness. The Knights of the Silver Hand are the legendary order of holy paladins founded after the First War to combine martial combat with the healing and smiting power of the Holy Light. Though their original northern chapter was broken during the fall of Lordaeron, surviving knights carry on their sacred vows in Stormwind and Ironforge, while scattered remnants battle the undead in the northern Plaguelands.

Following the destruction of Stormwind during the First War, Archbishop Alonsus Faol recognized a dire flaw in the Alliance's defenses: the clerics of Northshire were devoted and skilled healers, but they lacked martial training and fell easily on the front lines. To ensure holy warriors could endure the brutal combat of the Second War, Faol and his premier student, Uther the Lightbringer, founded the Order of the Knights of the Silver Hand in Stratholme. Faol recruited both battle-hardened knights willing to learn devotion to the Light and devout clerics willing to bear plate armor and warhammers.

The original five paladins—Uther the Lightbringer, Turalyon, Saidan Dathrohan, Tirion Fordring, and Gavinrad the Dire—proved instrumental to the Alliance of Lordaeron. First riding into combat during the Battle of Hillsbrad, the paladins lifted the morale of weary soldiers and countered the sinister necromancy of the Horde's death knights. Throughout the war, the Silver Hand broke peasant rebellions, reclaimed Caer Darrow, and helped defend Capital City against the siege of the orcs. In the years of peace that followed, the paladins guarded Lordaeron's borders, settled civil disputes, and served as shining exemplars of honor, humility, and justice.

Tragedy struck the order from within during the Third War. Prince Arthas Menethil, a decorated knight of the Silver Hand, clashed bitterly with his mentor Uther outside Stratholme and unlawfully suspended the paladins when Uther refused to butcher the infected citizenry. When Arthas later succumbed to corruption and led the Scourge against Lordaeron, Uther and Gavinrad were slain, shattering the order's central leadership. The surviving knights in the north fractured under differing doctrines, eventually birthing the zealous Scarlet Crusade and the vigilant Argent Dawn, while the surviving chapters in Stormwind and Ironforge continue to train new paladins under the classic banner of the Silver Hand.

Kobolds are diminutive, rat-like subterranean humanoids found scuttling through mines and caverns across Azeroth. Notorious for their obsessive devotion to the tallow candles strapped to their heads, they are individually cowardly but dangerous in swarms, fiercely defending their dig sites against any who threaten their light.

Standing barely four feet tall, kobolds are filthy, subterranean scavengers who spend their lives delving into the earth. Though they possess low-light vision, the deepest shafts are pitch-black, compelling every kobold to affix a crude candle to their head. While cowardly when cornered alone, kobolds breed in massive numbers and work with relentless energy. When agitated, their rat-like tails whip violently, and they overwhelm intruders in frantic mobs, beating foes to death with heavy iron mining picks.

To a kobold, a candle is far more than a light source; it is an existential shield. They harbor a deep, primal terror of the pitch-black tunnels, believing that the unlit darkness will actively consume them. Their leaders are frequently chosen by the length of the candle they bear, and their craftsmen harvest earwax and rendered fat to keep their wicks lit. Kobold folklore even treats the sun as the ultimate myth: the 'Wickless Candle,' a great eternal flame suspended from a vast blue cavern ceiling.

Across the Eastern Kingdoms, kobolds frequently overrun commercial mines. In Elwynn Forest, a clan displaced from the Redridge Mountains seized the Echo Ridge, Fargodeep, and Jasperlode mines, driven in part by Riverpaw gnolls and the Defias Brotherhood. In Loch Modan, the Tunnel Rat clan seized the Silver Stream Mine from the dwarven Miners' League. Even on Kalimdor, kobolds plague industrial digs, laboring for the Venture Company in Stonetalon or uncovering strange minerals in Thousand Needles.

Those who survived within the sealed lower levels were warped in mind and flesh by toxic fallout, mutating into pale, pustulant wretches dubbed leper gnomes.

King Llane Wrynn I was the ruler of Stormwind during the catastrophic First War, whose reign ended with the fall of the kingdom and his own tragic murder. A beloved and proud monarch, his steadfast refusal to believe his friend Medivh had betrayed humanity ultimately doomed his defense of the capital.

Born to King Barathen Wrynn, young Prince Llane grew up alongside Anduin Lothar and Medivh. When the Gurubashi trolls staged gruesome raids against Westfall settlements, Llane defied his father's defensive policies and led his companions into the jungles of Stranglethorn Vale to slay the warlord Jok'non. This bold defiance ignited an all-out Gurubashi invasion. Though Barathen perished leading a desperate counterattack outside the city gates, Medivh intervened with devastating sorcery to annihilate the troll vanguard. In the wake of this costly victory, Llane ascended to the throne as Stormwind's king.

When mysterious, green-skinned creatures emerged from the southern swamps, King Llane dispatched Lothar to investigate the Black Morass. What began as minor skirmishes erupted into the First War as the Horde overran Brightwood, Westfall, and Redridge. Messengers sent to Lordaeron and other northern human kingdoms were dismissed, their pleas undermined by Stormwind's historic isolationism and aristocratic intrigue. Despite these disadvantages, Llane organized an audacious counterattack alongside Lothar that broke the Horde's initial siege of Stormwind, dealing the invaders their first major defeat.

Llane's steadfast nature ultimately blinded him to the true danger within his inner circle. Even when Medivh's apprentice Khadgar and the emissary Garona revealed that the Guardian himself had opened the Dark Portal, Llane refused to accept his childhood friend's treachery. Soon after, Orgrim Doomhammer unified the Horde and breached Stormwind's outer defenses. As Llane directed the defense from Stormwind Keep, Garona—compelled by the magical influence of the Shadow Council—murdered the King in his own throne room, carving out his heart and sealing the city's doom.

Lordaeron takes its name from Lordain, a revered general of the ancient Empire of Arathor who sacrificed his life during the Troll Wars. Mages are scholarly spellcasters who bend the fabric of reality through arcane study, hurling destructive fire, controlling frost, and raw arcane energy. While physically fragile and cloaked only in cloth, their mastery over teleportation, conjuration, and battlefield crowd control makes them formidable allies and terrifying foes. Their discipline requires immense mental dedication, balancing immense destructive potential against the perilous history of arcane misuse.

The path of the mage demands intellect, focus, and years of rigorous study. Rather than communing with spirits or relying on divine faith, magi treat magic as a precise cosmic science. By drawing upon arcane energies, a practitioner can weave raw destructive power, summon searing bursts of flame, or chill the surrounding air into solid ice and howling blizzards. Because heavy armor disrupts the delicate somatic gestures and mental focus required for incantations, mages wear light cloth, relying instead on wards, mana barriers, and evasive spells to protect themselves.
The Legacy of Dalaran and Arathor

Human magical heritage began nearly three millennia ago during the Troll Wars, when high elven sorcerers instructed one hundred humans of the Empire of Arathor to turn the tide against the Amani. As the number of human practitioners multiplied, fearful mundane citizens drove many magi to establish the magocracy of Dalaran. Under the governance of the Kirin Tor, Dalaran became the central archive of magical study for the northern kingdoms, formalizing the traditions of combat magic that later supported the Alliance of Lordaeron through the First and Second Wars.

Arcane practitioners have never enjoyed uncomplicated trust. From the ancient cataclysm wrought by the Highborne to the catastrophic fall of Dalaran during the Third War, magic's volatile nature evokes widespread wariness. The Church of the Holy Light has historically treated wizardry with skepticism, and conservative knights have often viewed arcane spellcrafters as damned souls or a necessary evil on the battlefield. Despite this suspicion, civil and military leaders recognize that a capable magus offers invaluable battlefield supremacy, swift mass transportation, and essential countermeasures against supernatural threats.

Mages focus on three core schools: Arcane, Fire, and Frost. Arcane magic alters time, space, and reality, allowing for polymorphing, teleportation, and focused bursts of pure power. Fire spells focus on swift, overwhelming combustive damage to incinerate targets. Frost magic slows, snares, and shatters foes, providing critical battlefield control to keep enemies from closing into melee distance.

Murlocs are amphibious, bipedal humanoids famous for their gurgling battle cries, territorial coastal villages, and sudden swarming tactics. Though historically dwelling in the deep ocean, they have steadily migrated inland along the shores, lakes, and rivers of Azeroth, acting with far greater coordination and cunning than their primitive appearance suggests.

Murlocs dwell in densely populated settlements along coastlines, riverbanks, and freshwater lakes. Averaging roughly four feet in height, they possess bulbous, slime-coated bodies, wide mouths filled with sharp fangs, and keen vision capable of piercing pitch-black water. While individuals are rarely seen wandering far from their kin, encountering one murloc invariably means a dozen more lurk just beneath the surface. They rely on overwhelming numbers and sharp crude weaponry.

Though ancient lineages suggest murlocs have existed beneath the waves since before recorded history, their widespread encroachment onto the landmasses of Lordaeron and Kalimdor is relatively recent. Historians note that this inland migration coincided suspiciously with the reemergence of the serpentine naga from the ocean depths. Some tribes appear to worship deep-sea monstrosities waiting in the oceanic fathoms. Whether fleeing darker terrors or preparing the world for their masters' awakening, their coordinated movement into freshwaters poses a rising threat.

Because their garbled language sounds like nonsensical bubbling to outsiders, many dismiss murlocs as mere feral pests. However, their coordinated ambushes, mastery of earth and water magic, and communal structures hint at a sharper intellect. Renowned explorer Brann Bronzebeard has suggested that murlocs are far smarter than civilized races realize, intentionally concealing their cunning. Their impact on global history is undeniable: it was a murloc raid upon the Darkspear tribe that spurred Thrall to intervene, forging the alliance between the orcs and trolls that built the modern Horde.

Ten thousand years ago, in the ashes of the Great Sundering, Illidan Stormrage cast vials of the original Well of Eternity into a mountaintop lake atop Mount Hyjal, birthing a new font of arcane power. Nordrassil became the spiritual and cultural heart of night elf civilization through the blessings of three Great Dragon Aspects. Sounding the Horn of Cenarius, he called upon thousands of nature spirits and unleashed the stored enchantments within Nordrassil itself. The ensuing cataclysmic blast obliterated Archimonde and decimated the Legion. Though Nordrassil survived to heal slowly, its enchantments shattered—stripping the night elves of their beloved immortality.

Pirates and buccaneers are lawless seafaring plunderers operating across the Great Sea and coastal waters of Azeroth. Preying on Alliance, Horde, and neutral merchant vessels alike, they band together under loose flags to seize wealth, capture cargo, and control coastal coves. Their violent presence drives constant naval skirmishes from the waters of Kalimdor to the shores of the Eastern Kingdoms.

Pirates—often called buccaneers, corsairs, or freebooters—are maritime raiders of nearly every race who make their living seizing ships and raiding coastal settlements. Their operations stretch far beyond simple robbery; crews regularly engage in smuggling, kidnappings, and mercenary contracts for whoever has coin. With the chaos left behind by the Third War and the collapse of northern kingdoms, naval enforcement has fractured, giving pirate factions the freedom to carve out fortified footholds on neglected islands and coastal coves.

Despite common tales painting pirate life as one of romantic adventure, life aboard a buccaneer vessel is brutal and short. Crews endure squalid, rat-infested holds, harsh discipline, and the ever-present threat of scurvy, fought off only with supplies of limes. Betrayal is an everyday hazard, and captains maintain their command solely through strength and fear of punishment, which ranges from immediate execution to being marooned or fed to sharks. When battles end, buccaneers celebrate with roaring bouts of dice, song, and heavy rum.

While independent crews roam every sea lane, major organizations wield enough ships to contest sovereign navies. The Southsea Freebooters harass shipping throughout the waters surrounding Kalimdor, while the notorious Bloodsail Buccaneers menace the southern seas and wage open war against the Steamwheedle Cartel in Booty Bay.

The Plague of Undeath is a supernatural contagion concocted by the Lich King under the direction of the Burning Legion to scourge northern Eastern Kingdoms. Transmitted through infected grain, airborne cauldrons, and tainted waterways, the sickness rapidly kills living mortals and raises them as mind-bound thralls of the Scourge.

The plague was devised by the fallen shaman Ner'zhul after he was transformed into the Lich King by Kil'jaeden. From his icy seat atop the Frozen Throne in Northrend, Ner'zhul perfected the sickness as an unholy vanguard for the Burning Legion's invasion. Testing his power on isolated human villages across Northrend, he discovered that he could snuff out life and psychically command the corpses that arose shortly after. Ner'zhul's telepathic summon reached across the Great Sea to the Kirin Tor mage Kel'Thuzad, who abandoned Dalaran to serve the entity. Kel'Thuzad organized the secretive Cult of the Damned, whose mortal infiltrators laid the groundwork to poison Lordaeron from within.

Kel'Thuzad and the dreadlord Mal'Ganis chose Lordaeron's agricultural heartland to distribute the contagion. The cult secured distribution centers around Andorhal, packaging the plague into crates of grain destined for population centers across the north, including Brill and Stratholme. Unsuspecting villagers baked bread with the contaminated shipments, falling sick with burning joints, oozing sores, and milky eyes. Within three days, entire communities perished, only to immediately rise as flesh-eating zombies bound to the Lich King's psychic call. Prince Arthas Menethil raced to intercept the shipments, culminating in the horrific culling of Stratholme's citizens before the infected bread could transform them into Mal'Ganis's army.

The blight extends far beyond humanity. While non-human fauna generally suffer sickening fevers or rot rather than rising as undead thralls, the land itself bears the brunt of demonic and necromantic decay. Across the Plaguelands, massive plague cauldrons pump alchemical and magical vapors directly into the atmosphere, corrupting the surrounding land, where carrion grubs and colossal spore-choked mushrooms thrive. The Argent Dawn actively battles this airborne corruption by sabotaging these cauldrons, reversing their catalytic mixtures to burn the Scourge rather than feed it. Meanwhile, in the Undercity, the Royal Apothecary Society experiments tirelessly to refine a New Plague designed to slay both living foes and the undead.

Quilboar are aggressive, boar-like humanoids native to central Kalimdor, renowned for their sharp spinal quills and relentless territorial savagery. Claiming descent from the fallen demigod Agamaggan, they dwell within dense mazes of razor-sharp brambles across Durotar, Mulgore, and the Barrens. Quilboar revere Agamaggan, the colossal boar Ancient who perished battling the Burning Legion during the War of the Ancients ten thousand years ago. According to their sacred traditions, the quilboar are his mortal offspring. Where Agamaggan bled and died across central Kalimdor, enormous thorny vines erupted from the scorched earth, forming sprawling root-mazes that the quilboar treat as holy ground. His crystallized blood endures across the Barrens as crimson Blood Shards, which their geomancers dig up and revere as powerful talismans.

Rather than building traditional towns of stone or timber, quilboar cultivate colossal briars that choke surrounding vegetation and render nearby ground barren. Tribes are typically guided by powerful geomancers—practitioners of an earthbound, crude shamanism who consult stones and crystals to direct the clan. These mystics call upon Agamaggan's spirit to summon spectral boars into combat. Because the arid central plains offer few oases, quilboar view water as the ultimate treasure; they stage lavish feasts when rare rains fall and defend water holes with vicious tenacity.

Throughout the violent history of Azeroth, constant warfare has repeatedly driven civilian populations from their homes. Reorganizing their forces at Hearthglen and Tyr's Hand, they swore to cleanse the undead scourge with holy fire. Yet as the war dragged on, tragedy and suspicion festered within their ranks. Rejected by the zealots, Tyrosus and other disillusioned knights abandoned the order to form the Argent Dawn, remaining faithful to the pure, inclusive tenets of the Holy Light. Shan'do is a revered Darnassian honorific meaning "honored teacher" or "honored instructor." Traditionally used within night elven society and druidic circles, it denotes deep reverence toward a mentor who guides another along the path of wisdom and natural magic. Its direct counterpart is thero'shan, meaning "honored student."

In the Darnassian language, shan'do translates directly to "honored teacher" or "honored instructor." The prefix "shan" carries the meaning of honor, while the suffix "do" denotes authority, seniority, or mastery—a linguistic root shared with words like minn'do ("mother"). It is far more than an occupational label: addressing an elder or mentor as shan'do expresses solemn humility, filial devotion, and enduring respect for their guidance.

The title is most famously intertwined with the history of the Cenarion Circle. The demigod Cenarius was the original shan'do to Malfurion Stormrage, instructing him in the ways of nature before the War of the Ancients. In turn, Malfurion became shan'do to generations of mortal druids, to the point where "Shan'do Stormrage" is his standard styling among night elves, forest keepers, and reverent allies across Kalimdor.

While most common among Cenarion druids—such as disciples addressing Archdruid Naralex or the slumbering Malfurion—the honorific is fundamentally Darnassian, not exclusively religious. During the War of the Ancients, Illidan Stormrage briefly addressed the human sorcerer Rhonin as shan'do while learning from his peculiar arcane techniques. The title represents the bond of transmission between master and pupil, irrespective of the school of thought.

The Stonemasons Guild was the collective of master builders and artisans responsible for reconstructing Stormwind City and Nethergarde Keep after the Second War. Following a bitter dispute over payment with the House of Nobles that ended in deadly riots, the guild was forcibly dissolved, driving its members into exile and giving rise to the Defias Brotherhood.

Following the devastation of the First and Second Wars, the Alliance of Lordaeron commissioned the Stonemasons Guild to erect Nethergarde Keep in the Blasted Lands to monitor the shattered Dark Portal. Led by elected Guildmaster Edwin VanCleef, the artisans demonstrated a mastery of masonry that rivaled the Royal Stonecutters Union of the dwarves. Impressed by their labor, the House of Nobles hired the guild to embark upon the monumental task of rebuilding Stormwind City from ruins, trusting them to restore the capital to its ancient grandeur.

For years, VanCleef and an army of craftsmen toiled through Elwynn, raising the soaring spires of Stormwind Keep and the massive arches of the Cathedral of Light. However, royal finances collapsed under heavy military debts incurred in southern campaigns. The Kingdom of Stormwind is the southernmost and currently foremost human realm on Azeroth, holding dominion over Elwynn Forest, Westfall, Duskwood, and the Redridge Mountains. Sacked and shattered during the First War, it was rebuilt through blood and labor after the Second, rising to become the military and cultural center of the Alliance following the tragic collapse of Lordaeron in the north. Today, the kingdom stands beset from within and without, ruled by the ten-year-old King Anduin Wrynn under the watchful guidance of Highlord Bolvar Fordragon while its crowned monarch remains missing.

Stormwind was established over a thousand years ago by descendants of the ancient Arathi empire who ventured south beyond the crags of Khaz Modan into fertile, forested valleys. For centuries, the northern kingdoms dismissed Stormwind as an isolated, rural hinterland, even ignoring desperate pleas for aid during the Gnoll War. Led by King Barathen Wrynn, the realm defeated the gnolls and later the Gurubashi trolls alone, forging a culture fiercely proud of its self-reliance and the Light.

That independence was nearly extinguished when the Orcish Horde poured through the Dark Portal. Stormwind City burned to ash in the First War, its King Llane slain. The surviving populace fled north across the Great Sea led by Sir Anduin Lothar, rallying the northern realms into the Alliance of Lordaeron. Once the Orcish threat was crushed in the Second War, refugees returned home, hiring the Stonemasons Guild to rebuild their magnificent capital of white stone and blue banners. When the Scourge wiped out Lordaeron during the Third War, Stormwind became humanity's greatest remaining bastion.

Beneath its soaring towers, Stormwind struggles to govern its vast southern holdings. While Elwynn Forest remains relatively secure, neighboring regions like Westfall are swarming with outlaws, Redridge faces constant orc and gnoll incursions, and the darkened woods of Duskwood have fallen out of the realm's control. A bitter dispute between the House of Nobles and the Stonemasons sparked the violent Defias riot that took the life of Queen Tiffin, scattering displaced workers into open rebellion across the provinces.

The kingdom's instability deepened with the sudden, quiet disappearance of King Varian Wrynn while sailing to a diplomatic summit with the Horde at Theramore. To preserve fragile public order, the crown was placed on his ten-year-old son, Anduin Wrynn, with Highlord Bolvar Fordragon named Lord Regent. Yet royal authority is divided and stalled: the House of Nobles, guided closely by the enigmatic Lady Katrana Prestor, repeatedly vetoes military deployments, leaving local towns to fend for themselves while dangerous secrets fester within Stormwind Keep.

Formally, the crown belongs to King Anduin Wrynn, who took the throne as a ten-year-old child. Because he is a minor, real governmental authority is wielded by Highlord Bolvar Fordragon as Lord Regent, with heavy legislative counsel and oversight from Lady Katrana Prestor and the House of Nobles.

The Syndicate is a widespread human criminal organization founded and led by dispossessed nobles of the fallen kingdom of Alterac. Operating out of fortified strongholds across the Alterac Mountains, Hillsbrad Foothills, and the ruins of Stromgarde Keep, they wage an uncompromising war against both the Alliance and the Horde to restore their lost aristocracy.

When the kingdom of Alterac collapsed in dishonor following King Aiden Perenolde's treachery during the Second War, its aristocracy was stripped of land and title. Refusing to accept their exile, the remaining Alteraci nobility banded together under the late king's son, Prince Aliden Perenolde. Adopting distinctive orange bandanas and standardizing their ranks with hired thugs, highwaymen, and hedge wizards, they forged the Syndicate. To the outside world, they behave like common brigands, raiding caravans, ambushing travelers, and running extortion rings. In truth, their criminal enterprises exist solely to fund an organized effort to reconquer their ancestral domains and subjugate surrounding lands.

The Syndicate maintains entrenched footholds across northern Lordaeron. In the snowy Alterac Mountains, they fortified the ruined town of Strahnbrad and established encampments throughout the Uplands and Dandred's Fold. To the south, they hold the crumbling remnants of Durnholde Keep in the Hillsbrad Foothills, using it as a springboard to harass Southshore and raid supply routes. Further east across the Thoradin's Wall, Lord Falconcrest marshals an occupying Syndicate army inside the historic ruins of Stromgarde Keep in Arathi, actively battling the battered Stromgarde Militia for mastery over the Arathi Highlands.

Unlike ordinary outlaws, the Syndicate harbors grand ideological ambitions that earn them the hatred of almost every regional faction. They view the Alliance as mortal enemies who stole their rightful heritage, frequently targeting Southshore officials such as Magistrate Henry Maleb. Towards the Horde, their stance is openly supremacist: following the philosophies of Aedelas Blackmoore, they view orcs merely as beasts fit for slave labor and seek to rebuild the internment camp system. Sylvanas Windrunner's Forsaken execute captured Syndicate members on sight, while the clandestine thieves' guild of Ravenholdt wages a constant shadow war against their sloppy, arrogant operatives.

While the Syndicate's noble leaders believe they are fighting for human supremacy and their birthright, they are being steered from within by darker masters. Cultists belonging to the Argus Wake have thoroughly infiltrated their upper ranks, manipulating men like Lord Falconcrest into seizing Stromgarde Keep. Far from serving human interests, the Argus Wake ultimately reports to the Shadow Council based in Felwood's Jaedenar, using the Syndicate's armies and stolen territories as a mortal vanguard to clear the way for the Burning Legion.

For countless generations, the tauren lived as seasonal nomads wandering the arid plains of the Barrens, hunting the great kodo and listening for the voice of the Earth Mother. The Third War was the apocalyptic conflict that shattered the old world order just a few years ago. Orchestrated by the Burning Legion and unleashed through the Lich King's Plague of Undeath, the war saw the fall of the Kingdom of Lordaeron and the near-total destruction of Quel'Thalas before culminating in a desperate, unified stand at Mount Hyjal.

The war began subtly in northern Lordaeron, disguised as a virulent sickness carried in infected grain distributed from Andorhal. The tainted harvest did not merely slaughter its victims; it raised them as ravenous ghouls bound to the Lich King's will. Prince Arthas Menethil raced to stem the contagion alongside the Kirin Tor sorceress Jaina Proudmoore. Blinded by grief, fury, and dreadlord manipulations, Arthas purged the infected population of Stratholme before pursuing his foe to the frozen waste of Northrend. There, he took up the cursed runeblade Frostmourne, casting aside his soul. He returned south only to murder his father, King Terenas, delivering Lordaeron into the hands of the Scourge.

Empowered by death, Arthas crushed the high elven realm of Quel'Thalas to resurrect the necromancer Kel'Thuzad at the Sunwell. The undead army then laid siege to Dalaran, seizing the spellbooks necessary to summon the demon lord Archimonde into Azeroth. With the commander of the Burning Legion walking mortal soil, Dalaran was leveled in an arcane display of devastation. The Scourge had served its purpose as an advance guard, and the Burning Legion turned its sights toward the eternal power resting across the Great Sea.
The Flight West and Mount Hyjal

Guided by cryptic warnings from the mysterious Prophet—later revealed as the redeemed Guardian Medivh—Warchief Thrall led the New Horde across the Great Sea, while Lady Jaina Proudmoore evacuated surviving Alliance refugees. In ancient Kalimdor, the newcomers clashed with the reclusive night elves before all three factions recognized the supreme threat looming over them. Beneath the World Tree Nordrassil atop Mount Hyjal, mortals stood together against impossible odds. Archimonde was destroyed by ancestral wisps when he reached the tree, shattering the Legion's vanguard and ending the war.

Although Archimonde fell, the peace of 25 ADP is fragile and stained with loss. The Alliance of Lordaeron is gone, leaving the kingdom of Stormwind and Ironforge to anchor the southern Alliance while Lordaeron sits rotting as the Plaguelands. In Kalimdor, Thrall's Horde carved out Durotar, yet tensions with the newly allied night elves remain volatile. The Scourge endures in the northern ruins, and the freed undead—the Forsaken—now hold the catacombs of Capital City, waging a war of survival against both former masters and vengeful crusaders.

Corrupted by promises of godlike power, Queen Azshara and her Highborne cast spells through the Well of Eternity to bring Sargeras and his demonic legions into the world. The night elf resistance, joined by early mortal races, the dragonflights, and the Wild Gods, fought desperately to halt the invasion, culminating in the destruction of the Well and the Great Sundering.

Warlocks are spellcasters who bargain with dark powers, commanding demons, debilitating curses, and devastating fire and shadow magics. While deeply feared and distrusted by nearly every civilized society on Azeroth, some wield these forbidden arts in defense of their factions, turning the weapons of the Burning Legion against its own agents.

Where ordinary spellcasters see corruption and ruin, warlocks see opportunity. They achieve victory through calculated cruelty, striking from a distance while cloaked in shadow and fire. By siphoning the vital essences and souls of their enemies, warlocks fuel their most catastrophic rituals, raining brimstone from the sky and breaking minds with agonizing curses. Because they wear only simple cloth and possess little physical resilience, they rely on summoned horrors to intercept danger, willingly sacrificing demonic thralls to ensure their own survival.

A warlock's authority over the Twisting Nether begins with petty bargains and grows into iron domination. Novices learn to command mischievous imps to hurl flame, but as a practitioner's dark understanding deepens, they bind far deadlier entities: voidwalkers torn from shadowy depths to absorb physical punishment, seductive succubi capable of beguiling enemy minds, and ravenous felhunters that devour magical energies. Each summon demands dangerous ritual focus, for the Nether's denizens constantly test their masters for any flicker of weakness.

The roots of orcish demonology trace back to Draenor, where the demon lord Kil'jaeden seduced Gul'dan with the promise of supreme power. Gul'dan founded the secretive Shadow Council and transformed many shaman—starting with members of the Blackrock clan—into masters of fel magic. The rampant use of demonic magic withered Draenor's fertile plains into barren red wasteland, heralding the Old Horde's invasion through the Dark Portal. In human lands, the Kirin Tor forbade demonology and hunted down illicit summonings, yet ambitious mages regularly succumbed to the lure of untamed sorcery.

In the modern era, warlocks walk a razor's edge between utility and execution. In Stormwind, practitioners meet hidden away in gloomy tavern basements, far from the watchful eyes of the Cathedral of Light. In Orgrimmar, they cluster in the shadowed chasms of the Cleft of Shadows, kept under scrutiny by Thrall's shamanistic regime. While their methods invite revulsion, neither Alliance nor Horde can completely dismiss the devastating edge warlock magic offers on a hostile battlefield.

Warriors are the quintessential frontline combatants of Azeroth, mastering heavy plate armor, shields, and nearly every form of martial weaponry. Fueling their most devastating strikes with pure combat rage, they charge into the thick of battle to defend weaker allies or carve through enemy ranks. They are found across every race and civilization, serving as everything from stalwart city guards and royal champions to wandering mercenaries.

Warriors rely neither on divine prayers nor arcane incantations. Their power stems entirely from physical endurance, battlefield discipline, and an exhaustive mastery of weaponry. Clad in the heaviest plate mail, they dictate the frontline. Some fight behind towering shields to withstand punishing assaults and draw peril away from spellcasters and archers. Others step forward with two-handed polearms, axes, and greatswords, or wade into melee wielding a blade in each hand to cleave through whole formations.

In the furnace of battle, pain and blood ignite a warrior's inner fire. Known simply as rage, this resource swells as warriors inflict and absorb punishment. Rather than yielding to exhaustion or bleeding wounds, seasoned fighters channel this combat fury directly into bone-shattering strikes, sweeping whirlwinds of steel, and deafening battle cries that bolster nearby comrades while shattering enemy morale.

Unlike classes tied to specific creeds or elemental patrons, the warrior tradition is universal to every race on Azeroth. Stormwind relies on the disciplined knight-champions of the Brotherhood of the Horse, Ironforge marshals its stout Forgeguard, and the Horde rallies around orcish blademasters, tauren braves, and Forsaken Deathguards. Whether driven by honor, territorial defense, or cold coin, those who answer the call of arms form the unbroken backbone of every standing army.

The Warsong clan is one of the most ferocious and legendary fighting forces among the orcs, formerly led by the revered chieftain Grommash Hellscream. Having survived exile, the internment camps, and demonic corruption, the clan now operates primarily in Ashenvale as the Warsong Outriders, fiercely securing lumber for the fledgling Horde while clashing ceaselessly with the night elves.

Long before crossing into Azeroth, the Warsong forged their reputation across the open plains of Draenor through mobile wolf-rider tactics, breaking ogre empires through sheer tenacity. Their violent temperament was so feared that Warchief Blackhand kept them behind during the First War to prevent erratic rampages. They finally surged through the Dark Portal under Grommash Hellscream after the Second War, only to be stranded on Azeroth when Draenor collapsed. While other orcs languished in Alliance internment camps, the Warsong evaded capture, wandering the wilderness and clinging to their warlike spirit until Thrall united with Hellscream to forge the New Horde.

Upon arriving in Kalimdor during the Third War, Thrall ordered Hellscream and his clan into Ashenvale to harvest timber and establish an outpost. The intrusion enraged the night elves and the forest demigod Cenarius. Pushed to the brink of slaughter, the Warsong succumbed once more to the pit lord Mannoroth's demonic blood to prevail, slaying Cenarius in a frenzy of fel corruption. Thrall and his allies managed to purge Hellscream of the curse, culminating in a fateful showdown where Grom gave his life to destroy Mannoroth. His heroic sacrifice broke the demon blood curse forever, cementing the Warsong clan's place in Horde history.

The People's Militia is a grassroots defense force founded by Gryan Stoutmantle to protect Westfall's residents from the Defias Brotherhood. Westfall was once the breadbasket of the Kingdom of Stormwind, but Stormwind withdrew its troops and left the people defenseless.
